newsitem.title: UK: Mechanics of Britain's election as big day nears.
newsitem.headline: Mechanics of Britain's election as big day nears.

text.p: British election campaigns must last at least 17 days between the dissolution of parliament and polling day -- not including weekends, bank holidays and "days of public thanksgiving or mourning".
Apart from that stipulation, contained in the Parliament Act of 1911, the mechanics of the election are not cast in stone.
Following is a run-down of procedures for the election.
LENGTH OF PARLIAMENT
Britain elects a parliament for five years, but the prime minister has the power to cut its term short and call a new election.

If parliament is allowed to run its term, the election cut-off date is set as the first Thursday that follows the fifth anniversary of the opening of parliament plus 17 days, not including weekends and bank holidays.
The 1992 election was held on April 9 and parliament opened on April 27.

This means that Prime Minister John Major theoretically could delay the election until May 22, although he has said several times that it would in fact take place no later than May 1, the date of local elections in England.
DAY OF ELECTION
Only recent custom obliges Major to hold the election on a Thursday. The 1931 election took place on a Tuesday. Polling in 1922 and 1924 was on a Wednesday.
Thursday has been the day of elections since 1935, although by-elections were held on other days of the week as recently as the 1960s.
INFORMING THE QUEEN

In 1992 Major told waiting cameramen in Downing Street the date of the election immediately after returning from Buckingham Palace where, as the constitution dictates, he had asked Queen Elizabeth to dissolve parliament.
But, strictly speaking, the prime minister can keep the date to himself after he has told the monarch. In the 1950s, Downing Street officials said, a few days elapsed before the date was made public.
DISSOLUTION OF PARLIAMENT
It is usual for the prime minister to give several days' notice of the dissolution of parliament to allow time for vital remaining business to be completed.
This time the government will be eager to push through important education and police bills before parliament is dissolved.

Between 1945 and 1970, parliament was given 10 to 23 days' notice of its coming dissolution. But during the "Who governs Britain?" election of February 1974, Prime Minister Ted Heath announced the dissolution just 24 hours in advance.
Margaret Thatcher gave four and seven days' warning in 1983 and 1987, respectively, while Major provided five days' notice in 1992.
Polling takes place 17 working days after dissolution.
This means Major would have to dissolve parliament on March 12 -- with no prior notice -- if he wanted to go to the country on April 10.
If the monarch dies after the dissolution, polling day is postponed for two weeks.
TRANSITION OF POWER
If Major loses the election, he will be expected to leave his 10, Downing Street residence and office within minutes.
Oxford University Professor David Butler has called it "the swiftest transfer of power in the democratic world".
At the last handover in 1979, the Conservatives clinched victory at 2.45 pm on the Friday following polling day.
Anticipating defeat, outgoing Labour Prime Minister James Callaghan had been to Buckingham Palace at 2.30 pm and an hour later Thatcher had taken office as Britain's first woman prime minister.
ASSEMBLY OF NEW PARLIAMENT
Eighteen days elapsed in 1992 between polling day on April 9 and the assembly of the new parliament on April 27.
In 1979, 1983 and 1987, just six days elapsed.
WHO CAN VOTE?
Eligible to vote are 43.9 million out of 58 million inhabitants. The voting age is 18. Voting is not compulsory. In 1992, 77.8 percent of the electorate of 43.2 million voted.
